title: More, and most
goal: Use third-group adjectives, form the "more" and "most" degrees, compare with quam, and turn adjectives into adverbs.
bekal: use *fortis, forte* and its relatives with the right endings
memorize the six most common irregular sets: *bonus, melior, optimus* and friends

dialogs.title: Colloquium — Quis fortior est?
dialogs.intro: The debate that will never end: who is greater.

lines.speaker: Iulia:
lines.text: Minime! Tu celerior es, sed non fortior.
lines.id: Not at all! You're faster, but not stronger.
lines.literal: not-at-all! you faster are-you, but not stronger.

lines.speaker: Marcus:
lines.text: Celeritas melior est quam corpus magnum!
lines.id: Speed is better than a big body!
lines.literal: speed better is-it than body big-neut!

lines.speaker: Sextus:
lines.text: Ego non sum fortis. Sed felix sum!
lines.id: Well, I'm not strong. But I'm lucky!
lines.literal: I not am-I strong. but lucky am-I!

lines.speaker: Titus:
lines.text: Bene dicis, Sexte. Felicitas maxima res est.
lines.id: Well said, Sextus. Luck is the greatest thing of all.
lines.literal: well say-you, Sextus-call. luck biggest-fem thing is-it.

lines.speaker: Lydia:
lines.text: Magister, estne Roma maior quam Alexandria?
lines.id: Sir, is Rome bigger than Alexandria?
lines.literal: teacher-call, is-it-Q Rome bigger than Alexandria?

lines.speaker: Titus:
lines.text: Roma maxima urbium est. Sed Alexandria pulcherrima est.
lines.id: Rome is the biggest city. But Alexandria is the most beautiful.
lines.literal: Rome biggest-fem city-pl-of is-it. but Alexandria most-beautiful-fem is-it.

lines.speaker: Marcus:
lines.id: And who is the best poet?

lines.speaker: Titus:
lines.text: Vergilius optimus est. Sed Horatius brevior et acutior.
lines.id: Vergil is the best. But Horace is shorter and sharper.
lines.literal: Vergil best-masc is-he. but Horace shorter and sharper.

lines.speaker: Iulia:
lines.text: Liber Vergilii longissimus est — difficilior quam mons!
lines.id: Vergil's book is so long — harder than climbing a mountain!
lines.literal: book Vergil-of longest-masc is-it — harder than mountain!

lines.speaker: Titus:
lines.id: Difficult things are the more beautiful ones, Iulia.

lines.speaker: Marcus:
lines.id: Not really, sir! Easy things are better.

notes: **Fortior, celerior, pulchrior — one ending for "more".** The "more" degree is formed by adding *-ior* to the adjective stem: *fortis* → *fortior*, *longus* → *longior*, *pulcher* → *pulchrior*. The neuter form is *-ius*: *fortius*, *longius*. It works like English *-er* (stronger, longer), but Latin uses it for every adjective — there is no separate "more" for long words.

**Quam means "than".** *Fortior quam Sextus* — "stronger than Sextus". The thing compared takes the same form as the first. There is a shorter second way: drop *quam* and use the with/in form — *fortior Sexto*. Both mean the same, and writers use the second one more often.

**Maxima, pulcherrima, longissimus — the "most" degree.** The ending is *-issimus*, but words ending in *-er* take *-errimus* (*pulcher* → *pulcherrimus*, *acer* → *acerrimus*), and six words ending in *-ilis* take *-illimus* (*facilis* → *facillimus*, *difficilis* → *difficillimus*). The "most" degree can also mean "very": *longissimus* can be "longest" or simply "very long".

**Difficilia, facilia, meliora — adjectives standing alone.** The neuter plural is used to talk about "things that are…": *difficilia* means "difficult things". You have already seen this pattern with *multa*, *cetera*, and *vera*.

blocks.text: Besides the *bonus, bona, bonum* group you already know, there is a second group that uses third-declension endings. Its members are some of the most common words: *fortis*, *omnis*, *gravis*, *facilis*, *dulcis*, *felix*, *ingens*.

So masculine and feminine share the same forms, and only the neuter differs. These are called two-ending adjectives. There are also one-ending ones — a single subject form for all three genders — and three-ending ones.
Both degrees are built on the adjective's stem, which is the "of" form minus its ending. For *longus, longa, longum* the stem is *long-*; for *fortis, fortis* it is *fort-*.

The "more" degree changes its endings like an ordinary third-group adjective, but its neuter ends in *-ius*, not *-ior*: *liber longior* but *verbum longius*. The "most" degree changes like *bonus*: *longissimus, longissima, longissimum*.
All six already live in English: *optimal*, *pessimist*, *maximum*, *minimum*, *plus*, *proximity*, *major*, *minor*, *ameliorate*. If you're unsure, think of the English word.
Adverbs of manner — "quickly", "well" — are made from adjectives by swapping the ending, much like English *-ly*. Just two rules, one for each adjective group.

The "more" degree of an adverb is always the same as the neuter "more" form: *fortius* ("more bravely"), *clarius* ("more clearly"), *melius* ("better"). The "most" degree ends in *-issime*: *fortissime*, *clarissime*, and the irregular *optime*, *pessime*, *maxime*, *minime*.

blocks.title: Words you already use every day
items: *Minime* — which you have used for "not at all" since Unit 1 — actually means "least".
*Maxime* means "most, especially", and it gives us *maximal*.
*Optime!* was everyday Roman praise: "excellent!" Its opposite is *pessime*.
*Gratias maximas* — "the greatest thanks" — is the most polite way to say thank you in Latin.

exercises.prompt: Form the "more" degree (-ior) of these adjectives.

items: Liber tuus ____ est quam liber meus. (better)

answers: longior — fortior — gravior — pulchrior — felicior — brevior
longissimus — fortissimus — pulcherrimus — facillimus — optimus — maximus
celerior — maxima — melior — brevissima — minor — severissimus
clare — fortiter — celeriter — bene — male — feliciter
